Once you get something out of the dungeon, you don't unlock it permanently for use, instead if you bring that mercenary or card to the dungeon and die with it, you lose the card. I think it would be more fun if you just unlocked it permanently and that's it, why make the player take a risk, there's no real long term progress this way.

一句话建议：先刷各个+15+20+30容量遗物（每层boss也有），刷到之后不要吝啬于小退sl改变世界线和用ce修改钱和血量，一定要用尽盘外招活着带出来；熬到进本能有100以上cost再按照其他评论的流派认真玩，不然你刷到的、强化好的核心卡、遗物、随从根本带不出来，下一局也带不进去，全是无效劳动。 初见杀问题：弱引导导致初见杀太多了，比如“路过每层只有一两个的出口时如果不撤离，出口节点就会消失，无法回踩只能从下一个出口离开”（我可以理解移动加压力值，也可以理解节点不能回踩，但是两件折磨的事情重合到一起，还是第一次见。）；偏偏这游戏选择了撤离类玩法，如果玩家没法顶着越来越高的压力打到下一个出口就会全身白给。他的压力系统是走的步数越多，遇到小怪数量就越多；一个尖塔20层玩家前期可以打过3只怪但很难用不成体系的废卡打过一波又一波的7怪8怪（这里甚至没有考虑随从死亡的成本），这么重要的设定非要用人命去试出来实在是太不应该了。 从“撤离”的角度说，虽然宣传一直在擦“撤离”的边，但是这游戏的局外要素没有多少，至少还没有暗黑地牢和奇妙探险队多（而负面事件的不讲理程度却追平了后者）；没有局外天赋类加点、金币只用于通关评分无法带出局外、物品卡牌带出来不容易带进去限制却更大。很多人不喜欢尖塔like有局外养成，ok fine，那么为了讨好这部分玩家要牺牲被“撤离”吸引来的玩家，是否挂羊头卖狗肉了呢。 从“爬塔”的角度来说，从图鉴看到全卡池之后，玩家会感叹卡池不仅浅，还填充以大量近似替代卡和完全替代卡，这意味着如果不再更新卡池的话，主流构筑屈指可数。而当我看到两张从名字到效果都一样的“盾击”卡时难免会有些不太好的猜想。 关于物品带出带入限制方面具体来说，如果你中期带着6件以上的容量遗物，选最高的两个难度，带着多张核心卡打到第二层可以以400+的cost美美带出一局的所有收益，但是下一次进本还是只能携带100出头的cost。一个强力遗物就要几十cost，30+cost的随从更是想都不敢想。至于前期嘛。。。你打到、甚至sl刷到若干张构筑核心卡，活到了出口，看着那60左右的cost，意味着你只能带1个遗物加3张卡出去，其他的全都扔掉。。。你会再次感受到初见杀的恶毒。

Though once you get the hang of it and built a crazy deck, you can basically solo everything. (P.S. Cast on draw all the way)

I've played a lot of deck builders and this one has my favorite concept and gameplay so far. It's very fun to farm for a team and items that works well together. For new players my advice is farm all of the capacity relics first and focus on getting back to base with them. The game gets way more fun when you can take a lot into the start of a run.

its brutal, and its good. update: so... at 40-ish hours, i've realized, it's not just good, its great. and the dev is active and responsive and actually fixes things that are being reported, pretty quickly, which is a plus, but really, it is a very good game, you'll easily get over 100hrs if you actually want to try different builds and not just stick to a single one. but if you stick to a single build, around 50 hours. maybe 60. that's how much content it offers at base. and that is if you're very good at the game and don't lose often. if you do lose a lot, it could take 80-100 hours just to complete all difficulty levels, which you are actually incentified to do, because it actually matters in your progression and leveling. its a very good design for a roguelike/lite deckbuilder. its just really well designed for such a small indie game. kudos to the author for the wonderful work.

Gold and Graves, developed and published by Yoon, is a smartly designed indie strategy game that blends roguelike structure, deckbuilding mechanics, and turn-based tactical combat into a cohesive and distinctive experience. While it borrows familiar elements from several well-known genres, it sets itself apart through a clever central idea: enemies are not just obstacles to be eliminated, but potential assets to be recruited. This single design choice reshapes how players approach combat, risk, and progression, giving the game a personality that feels thoughtful rather than derivative. At the core of the experience is a dungeon-crawling loop built around grid-based, turn-based battles. Each encounter plays out on a clear tactical board where positioning, turn order, and ability timing matter greatly. Instead of simply attacking until enemies fall, players are encouraged to weaken foes strategically and then use gold to bribe them into joining their side. Once recruited, these former enemies become controllable units with their own abilities, strengths, and weaknesses. This creates a constant tension between spending gold as a resource and preserving it for future growth, as every bribe is both an investment and a risk. Deckbuilding adds another important layer to this system. Cards represent actions, abilities, and tactical options, and the composition of your deck directly affects how battles unfold. New cards and relics are earned during dungeon runs and can be carried forward between attempts, gradually expanding the range of strategies available. Synergies between cards, recruited mercenaries, and relic effects form the heart of the game’s long-term appeal, rewarding experimentation and careful planning. Runs rarely feel identical, as even small changes in deck composition or ally selection can significantly alter how encounters play out. One of the most compelling aspects of Gold and Graves is its approach to progression and risk management. Rather than forcing players to push a run to its absolute limit, the game allows you to retreat voluntarily from the dungeon. Escaping successfully lets you bring back collected resources, allies, and upgrades to strengthen future attempts. This extraction-based structure introduces meaningful decision-making: pushing deeper promises greater rewards but also increases danger, while retreating early may feel safer but less efficient. Knowing when to leave becomes just as important as knowing how to fight. As time passes during a run, the dungeon grows increasingly hostile. A rising danger level introduces tougher enemies and more punishing encounters, discouraging players from stalling or farming indefinitely. This system keeps momentum high and ensures that every decision carries weight. The balance between greed and caution is a constant presence, and many of the game’s most memorable moments arise from narrowly escaping with hard-earned gains or losing everything due to one overly ambitious choice. Visually, Gold and Graves adopts a clean, readable 2D art style that prioritizes clarity over spectacle. The grid-based maps are easy to parse, making tactical positioning intuitive even during complex encounters. Character and enemy designs fit well within a dark fantasy aesthetic without becoming overly detailed or distracting. The interface is functional and streamlined, allowing players to focus on strategy rather than fighting menus. Sound design and music support the atmosphere without overpowering the experience, reinforcing tension during battles and exploration. The game does demand patience and a willingness to learn. Its systems interlock tightly, and understanding how cards, mercenaries, relics, and dungeon mechanics interact takes time. Early runs may feel punishing as players experiment and make mistakes, but this learning process is part of the intended experience. For players who enjoy gradually mastering layered systems and refining strategies over multiple attempts, the challenge feels rewarding rather than frustrating. Overall, Gold and Graves is a confident and well-crafted fusion of ideas that manages to feel fresh through its emphasis on recruitment, extraction, and tactical depth. It does not rely on flashy presentation or narrative exposition to engage the player, instead building satisfaction through smart mechanics and meaningful choices. For fans of roguelikes, deckbuilders, and tactical strategy games who enjoy risk management and experimentation, it offers a deeply engaging experience that rewards careful thought and repeated play. Rating: 8/10

1,创意很不错，值得称赞和鼓励。 2，损失厌恶太高，无法忍受。 3，细节过于繁琐，缝合太多，不是什么类型都适合搜打撤，元素内容过多，反而会影响游戏体验。 4，游戏内成本支出过高，干什么都要支出，都要算计，不仅过度消耗思考成本，同样叠加过多损失厌恶。 5，其实只要英雄无敌+杀戮尖塔模式，就足够我玩一阵了。但狗尾续貂弄个搜打撤，所以差评。 6，制作者不明白卡牌元素有一些核心感受，即“收集欲”和“占有欲”，搜打撤彻底毁了卡牌的收集期待，感受不对，游戏崩溃。 其实各行各业都有类似的东西。明明很有创意，明明很好，但核心感受被破坏，就没人买账。这游戏发行了近半年，成绩不行，这个是主要原因。 卡牌，遗物，佣兵，三个核心元素，全无法“收集”和“占有”，那我玩个什么？ 每次玩，都要各种限制，强化的卡牌只能用一次，这可比氪金手游更黑。 如果只有一种损失厌恶，可以理解，但这游戏所有元素的损失厌恶加一起，高得可怕，只适合M玩。 7，建议：如果制作者不缺钱，不想盈利，那就坚持初心。如果制作者想要平衡收益，建议彻底放弃搜打撤，或者换皮制作新游戏，给足玩家安全感。 如果要平衡感受，建议，在卡牌、遗物、佣兵、强化四个元素中，选其一进行搜打撤，其余不要都这么做，或者像杀戮尖塔那样，减少“游戏内支出成本”。 比如建议佣兵不死。玩家考虑的是游戏的乐趣，而不是一边战斗，一边要花钱买佣兵，一边还要担心佣兵死。 英雄无敌是会死，但有足够的安全感。 这种毫无安全感的游戏，彻底破坏了卡牌类游戏的乐趣。
还是好玩的，就是很容易让人突然破防，提醒一下，进入随机节点遇见恶心事件或者打boss感觉要死的时候，可以点esc保存并退出，然后就可以重新回到进入节点前sl了，感觉带进去的东西全部都要占背包是个败笔，不如改成带进去的遗物或者佣兵或者卡牌之中的一样带出时不算，好歹玩家心里舒服一点
